claims.text: Adding a minor fraction of boron to a conventional metallic-glass-forming alloy enhances its glass-forming ability.
The enhancement in glass-forming ability results from increased atomic packing frustration.
A typical unmodified Zr–Cu–Ni–Al metallic-glass precursor has limited glass formation under standard cooling conditions.
Approximately 2–5 atomic percent boron is an appropriate addition to the base alloy.
Boron atoms are small relative to the constituent atoms of the proposed metallic-glass alloy.
Boron has bonding characteristics different from those of the base-alloy constituents.
The size and bonding characteristics of boron disrupt local atomic order.
Boron introduces atomic-size mismatch and unique chemical interactions into the alloy.
The atomic-size mismatch and chemical interactions introduced by boron increase local packing frustration.
Increased local packing frustration raises the nucleation barrier for crystals during cooling.
The boron-doped alloy will have a higher amorphous-phase fraction than the undoped alloy.
The boron-doped alloy will have an increased critical cooling rate for glass formation relative to the undoped alloy.
Under identical processing conditions, the undoped alloy has a lower amorphous-phase fraction.
Under identical processing conditions, the undoped alloy has a greater tendency to crystallize.
The proposed effect applies primarily to metallic systems in which atomic-size mismatch can be exploited.
Boron addition may not produce the same effect in nonmetallic glass systems.
Successful boron doping is expected to elevate the crystallization-onset temperature relative to the control.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims enhanced glass-forming ability and a higher barrier to crystal nucleation, but the predicted outcome specifies an increased critical cooling rate. Enhanced glass-forming ability is ordinarily represented by a lower required critical cooling rate, so this outcome is directionally inconsistent with the stated mechanism and overall hypothesis.
